古高.note: A loyalist agent (1829–1864) who, under the merchant alias Masuya Kiemon, ran an arms depot for the Chōshū-aligned plotters. His arrest set off the Ikedaya raid.

岸淵兵輔.note: A Mito clansman, once a visitor at Kondō’s Edo dōjō, here made the bearer of the first warning about the Masuya. Romanization mine.

四国屋.note: Shōkuōya Jūbei, keeper of the Kiyamachi restaurant Tantora, a known haunt of the Chōshū and Tosa men.

島田魁.note: A Shinsengumi inspector, one of the biggest men in the corps; served on the surveillance of the Masuya.

周平.note: Kondō Shūhei, Kondō Isami’s adopted son, one of the five who charged into the Ikedaya.

渡辺幸右衛門.note: The beat constable who, being on friendly terms with the corps, passed the tip to Mibu rather than to his own office. Romanization mine.

利助.note: A newly hired servant of the Masuya who informed on the arms cache. Romanization mine.

熊坂長範.note: The giant bandit of medieval legend, a stock figure of the theater; see the note in the chapter.

枡屋.note: The tool-and-sundries shop that was the front for Furutaka’s arms depot.

茨木屋.note: The sundries-wholesaler on Kawaramachi from whose upper floor the corps kept watch on the Masuya.

丹虎.note: A Kiyamachi restaurant kept by Shikokuya Jūbei, the second suspected meeting-place; the object of Toshizō’s party on the night of the raid.

池田屋.note: The inn at the west end of Sanjō-kobashi, kept by one Sōbei, where the loyalists met and where Kondō’s party struck.

本圀寺.note: A temple on Horikawa used as the Kyōto quartering-ground of the Mito clan’s troops.

三条小橋.note: The “little bridge” on Sanjō, over the Takase canal; the Ikedaya stood at its west end.

ch22.note: The era-name changed from Bunkyū to Genji early in 1864; the first year of Genji is 1864. The first day of the sixth month by the old lunar calendar fell on 4 July, and the Ikedaya raid four nights later on 8 July.

ch22.anchor: an Ōharame had passed along Kawaramachi
ch22.note: The ōharame were women from Ōhara, north of Kyōto, who carried firewood and charcoal-logs (kuroki) into the city on their heads to sell, in a dress of their own with white leggings. Their sing-song cry was a fixture of the Kyōto street.

ch22.anchor: the mimed Kumasaka Chōhan of the Mibu mystery plays
ch22.note: The Mibu kyōgen are wordless Buddhist morality-plays mimed to gong and drum at the Mibu-dera, near the corps’s own barracks. Kumasaka Chōhan is the giant robber of medieval legend, killed while raiding an inn; in the mime he lumbers about in an outsized mask. Okita’s private joke is that the harder the dreaded Toshizō scowls, the more he looks like that comic ogre.

The coup of the eighteenth day of the eighth month, 1863 (the third year of Bunkyū). Satsuma and Aizu, backing the moderates at court, drove the radical Chōshū faction out of Kyōto overnight; seven Chōshū-aligned court nobles fled with them to the west in the “flight of the seven nobles.” It is this humiliation that the Chōshū plotters of the Ikedaya mean to reverse. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: the disguise assumed by Furutaka Shuntarō
ch22.note: Historical. Furutaka Shuntarō (1829–1864), a rural samurai of Ōmi and a shrine-retainer of the Bishamon-dō monzeki (an imperial-abbot temple), ran an arms depot in Kyōto under the merchant name Masuya Kiemon, supplying the plot to fire the city and carry the Emperor off to Chōshū. His seizure is the hinge of the whole affair. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: suffered torture past the power of words, but in the end confessed nothing
ch22.note: Here Shiba takes a deliberate line on a disputed point. The famous tradition, which comes down from the early Shinsengumi chroniclers, has Furutaka broken under brutal torture at the Mibu barracks — hung upside down with a spike through his feet — and made to confess the fire-and-abduction plot, which then triggered the raid. Shiba instead has him hold out and gives the credit to the covenant-roster (renpanjō) seized at the shop, by which the conspirators’ names were already known. The seizure and killing are certain; how much the raid owed to torture as against captured documents is what the accounts dispute.

ch22.anchor: The storming of the Ikedaya was at the Hour of the Boar
ch22.note: The Ikedaya Incident, the night of the fifth day of the sixth month, Genji 1 — 8 July 1864. A handful of Shinsengumi under Kondō surprised a war-council of Chōshū, Tosa, and other loyalists at the inn and, after a two-hour fight, killed or took some dozens of them for the loss of few of their own. The raid broke the planned rising, made the Shinsengumi’s name across the country, and hardened the road to the Chōshū war that followed within the month. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: in a letter Kondō sent to his adoptive father Shūsai in Edo
ch22.note: The passages that follow are quoted from Kondō Isami’s own letters to his adoptive father Kondō Shūsai, real documents in the stiff epistolary Japanese of the day; Shiba’s bracketed insertions (“passage omitted,” the gloss on the hours, “my adopted son”) are his. They are among the closest first-hand records of the fight, and their boasting tone is Kondō’s.

ch22.anchor: a hemp haori bearing the light-blue mountain-stripe
ch22.note: The Shinsengumi’s notorious uniform: a light-blue (asagi) hemp overcoat with a jagged “mountain-stripe” (dandara) hem, worn here over a leather fencing-cuirass, a mail undershirt, and an iron brow-guard. Shiba’s closing detail is a relic’s: the very brow-guard Toshizō wore, with two sword-cuts in it, was preserved in the Hijikata family house at Ishida in Hino. Corroborated.
